cards.html:
This skill ties the track together in one realistic decision, from question to recommendation, and ends with a checklist of the mistakes to avoid. Work through it as a review: each step points back to the skill where it was taught.

Key wordPlain meaning
Fixed-price bidA promise to deliver for a set price, so overruns come out of your profit
PenaltyA charge for every day the project runs late
Decision ruleA limit agreed in advance, such as "at most a 15% chance of a loss"
Back-testChecking a model's predictions against what actually happened before
NewsvendorThe classic problem of how much stock to order before demand is known

A consultancy is asked to deliver a project for a fixed price of 300,000. Should it accept? The decision metric is expected profit together with the probability of a loss, because the partners have said they will not take a bid with more than a 15% chance of losing money (skill 2, step 1).

The model:

cost = 800 × days + materials
       + penalty
penalty = 1,000 × (days over 260)

Inputs, from past projects and the delivery lead:

InputDistributionWhy
Labour daysTriangular, min 180, mode 222, max 320Expert range, skewed to overruns
MaterialsLognormal, median 60,000, σ = 0.3Positive, multiplicative uncertainty
DependenceCorrelation 0.5 between themScope creep raises both
Day rateFixed at 800Contracted

The "plan" uses the most likely values: 800 × 222 + 60,000 = 237,600, a profit of 62,400. That is the number the sales team wants to quote.

from scipy.stats import norm, triang
rng = np.random.default_rng(99)
n = 200_000
C = [[1, .5], [.5, 1]]
z = rng.multivariate_normal(
    [0, 0], C, n)
u = norm.cdf(z)
days = triang.ppf(u[:, 0],
                  0.3, 180, 140)
mat = 60_000 * np.exp(0.3*z[:, 1])
late = np.maximum(days - 260, 0)
cost = 800*days + mat + 1_000*late
profit = 300_000 - cost

The Gaussian copula links the two inputs (skill 2). The triangular c = (222 − 180)/140 = 0.3. The materials draw uses the normal z directly, which is a lognormal with median 60,000. A seed is fixed and recorded (skill 3).

OutputValue
Expected profit39,400 (MCSE about 100)
P50 cost252,000
P80 cost295,000
P(loss)0.182 (MCSE 0.0009)
P5 profitabout −52,000
Plan profit (most likely inputs)62,400

Reading it:

  • The flaw of averages, in full (skill 6): the plan says 62,400; the expected profit is 39,400. Skewed days, the convex late penalty and correlation all push cost up.
  • The decision: P(loss) is 18%, above the 15% limit. As quoted, the bid fails the partners' rule.
  • Precision is ample (skill 4): with MCSE 0.0009 the 18% is not close to 15% in noise terms; 200,000 runs is more than enough.
  • Dependence matters (skill 6): with the correlation set to 0, P(loss) falls to 15.6%, close to the limit. Ignoring scope creep's common effect would have made a failing bid look borderline.

What would change the answer? A sensitivity run is the next step: labour days have the strongest link to profit (rank correlation −0.91, against −0.78 for materials, which share the scope-creep driver), so the levers are a tighter scope (cutting the upper tail of days), a higher price, or a cap on the late penalty. Each is one line to change and rerun with common random numbers (skill 3), so the comparison is sharp.

Before this goes to the partners:

  • Set every input to its mode: cost must be 237,600 (it is).
  • Check the marginals: days have mean (180 + 222 + 320)/3 ≈ 240.7 and the copula did not change it; materials have median 60,000.
  • Check the guard: what share of runs pays a penalty? It is 26%, which is plausible; 0% or 100% would point to a bug.
  • Back-test: did past fixed-price projects lose money about as often as the model says?
  • Rerun with another seed: P(loss) should agree within about 0.002.

CheckSkillThe mistake it prevents
Is the question tied to a decision and a metric?2Simulating everything, deciding nothing
Is every input range honest (P10 to P90, not min to max)?2, 6Too-narrow inputs, false confidence
Are common causes modelled as correlation or shared shocks?2, 6Thin tails on totals
Are shapes right for the support and tails?2, 6Negative durations, clipped values, normal losses
Is the model applied run by run, never to averaged inputs?6The flaw of averages
Is the seed fixed in advance, and are parallel streams spawned?3Irreproducible or duplicated runs
Is N planned from a pilot for the precision the decision needs?4Too few runs, or wasted compute
Is every result reported with its MCSE and sensible rounding?1, 4False precision

CheckSkillThe mistake it prevents
Are rare-event and tail estimates backed by enough hits?4, 5P99.9 from five points
Was a known-answer test and a back-test run?2, 6, 8Bugs and model bias
Is the method right (formula, bootstrap, MCMC)?7Simulating what has a formula; naive MCMC errors
Is the P50 labelled as a median, not as the plan?6Committing to a coin flip

A good simulation starts from a decision, models the real structure and links between inputs, reports estimates with their errors, is checked against known answers and history, and ends with a clear recommendation that shows the risk, not just one number.

Exercise. Order quantity for a seasonal product. A retailer sells a winter jacket for 25; each costs 10, and unsold jackets are cleared at 4. Demand is lognormal with median 1,000 (σ = 0.4), and there is a 10% chance a competitor launches and cuts demand by 30%. Simulate 100,000 seasons with seed 31 and evaluate order quantities 800 to 1,600 in steps of 100, using the same demand draws for every quantity. Report the best quantity, its expected profit, and whether the difference between 1,100 and 1,200 is real. Then compare with ordering "average demand".

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

Expected profit peaks at q = 1,200 (about 12,370), with 1,300 close behind (12,330). Because all quantities share the same demand draws (common random numbers), the gain from 1,100 to 1,200 is 108 with MCSE about 3: clearly real, even though each profit alone has an MCSE of about 15. Mean demand is about 1,050, so "order the average" leaves money on the table. The theory agrees: the best q is the demand quantile at the critical ratio (25 − 10)/(25 − 4) ≈ 0.714, which is about 1,220. A bigger order also has a worse bad case (P5 profit falls from 4,205 at q = 1,000 to 3,005 at 1,200), a trade-off to show the decision maker.

rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
n = 100_000
z = rng.normal(size=n)
d = 1000 * np.exp(0.4 * z)
hit = rng.random(n) < 0.10
d = np.where(hit, 0.7 * d, d)
def profit(q):
    sold = np.minimum(q, d)
    left = q - sold
    return 25*sold + 4*left - 10*q
for q in range(800, 1700, 100):
    print(q, profit(q).mean())
g = profit(1200) - profit(1100)
print(g.mean(), g.std() / n**0.5)

1. In the case study, why is the expected profit (39,400) so far below the plan (62,400)?
  2. P(loss) is 0.182 with MCSE 0.0009. Do you need more runs to compare it with the 15% rule?
  3. Setting the correlation to 0 gave P(loss) = 15.6%. Which result should be presented, and why?
  4. Name two validation checks you would run before presenting.
  5. The partners ask for "the number". What do you give them?

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

1: Skewed labour days, a convex late penalty and positive correlation all raise expected cost; the plan uses most likely values, so it suffers the flaw of averages. 2: No: the gap of 3.2 points is over 30 MCSEs. 3: The correlated one, because scope creep really drives both inputs; the independent run is a sensitivity case that shows how much the dependence matters. 4: Any two of: modal inputs give 237,600; marginals have the intended mean and median; the penalty share is plausible; a second seed agrees within MCSE; a back-test against past fixed-price projects. 5: Not a single number: expected profit 39,000, an 18% chance of loss (above the 15% limit), the P80 cost of 295,000, and the levers (price, scope, penalty cap) that would bring the risk under the limit.

quiz.q: Your P95 jumps noticeably every time you rerun with a new seed. What is most likely wrong?
o: too few runs for that tail: few runs lie beyond the P95
quiz.why: Tail percentiles need enough runs beyond them; plan N or use variance reduction.

quiz.q: Which method for estimating a 1-in-10,000 event within a few percent?
o: importance sampling (or very many plain runs)
quiz.why: Plain sampling needs about 100/p = 1 million runs for 10% error; importance sampling needs far fewer.

quiz.q: Plain sampling: how many runs for 10% relative error on p = 1/10,000?
quiz.why: About 100 hits needed: N ≈ 100/p = 1,000,000.

quiz.q: A bid's plan uses most likely inputs and shows profit 62,400; the simulation's mean is 39,400. The gap is mainly …
o: the flaw of averages: skew, a convex penalty and correlation
quiz.why: With MCSE around 100, the gap is model structure, not noise.

quiz.q: P(loss) = 0.182 with MCSE 0.0009. How many MCSEs above a 15% limit is it? (whole number)
quiz.why: (0.182 − 0.150)/0.0009 ≈ 36: no need for more runs.

quiz.q: If two scenarios differ by less than their MCSEs, the better-looking one should be chosen.
quiz.why: Myth. The difference is noise; use common random numbers or more runs to resolve it.

quiz.q: You compare order quantities 1,100 and 1,200. The sharpest comparison uses …
o: the same demand draws for both (common random numbers)
quiz.why: Shared draws make the noise cancel in the difference.

quiz.q: Price 25, cost 10, salvage 4. What is the newsvendor critical ratio (25 − 10)/(25 − 4)? (3 decimals)
quiz.why: 15/21 ≈ 0.714: order up to that demand quantile.

quiz.q: Ordering the average demand maximises expected profit for a seasonal product.
quiz.why: Myth. The best order is the demand quantile at the critical ratio, here about the 71st percentile.

quiz.q: Eight parallel workers give suspiciously smooth results and a tiny MCSE. First check?
o: whether workers share a seed (count distinct first draws)
quiz.why: Duplicated streams make runs repeat and the MCSE too small.

quiz.q: A pilot gives s = 400. Runs needed for a 95% half-width of 10? (nearest hundred)
MCSE of a mean with outcome SD 400,000 and 500 runs? (nearest thousand)
Durations are drawn from a normal and negative values are clipped to 0. The fix is …
o: use a positive distribution such as lognormal or gamma
quiz.why: A distribution with the right support avoids silent bias from clipping.

quiz.q: Labour and materials overruns share a cause. The model should …
o: link them with correlation or a common shock
quiz.why: Ignoring the common cause understates the tail of total cost.

quiz.q: A P50 cost is a sensible committed budget.
quiz.why: Myth. It is exceeded half the time; commit to a stated percentile such as P80 and show the range.

quiz.q: Your MCMC posterior mean has a naive s/√N error bar. What should you use instead?
o: an error bar based on effective sample size or batch means
quiz.why: Autocorrelated draws carry less information than their count suggests.

quiz.q: A risk model's 99.9th percentile is reported from 5,000 runs. The main problem?
o: it rests on about 5 runs beyond it
quiz.why: 0.1% of 5,000 is 5 runs: far too few to estimate that tail.

quiz.q: Before presenting, which check catches a logic bug fastest?
o: set inputs to fixed values with a known answer
quiz.why: A deterministic case with a known result isolates the logic from randomness.

quiz.q: You have 4 workers and spawn streams from SeedSequence(2026). How many numbers must you record to reproduce the whole run?
quiz.why: The parent seed reproduces every child stream.

quiz.q: A one-hour-per-run engineering model needs a tail probability. Best plan?
o: a fitted surrogate or a small designed experiment, with importance sampling where possible
a single run at average inputs
quiz.why: Expensive models need fewer, smarter runs; a single average-input run suffers the flaw of averages.

quiz.q: A small MCSE proves the model's inputs are right.
quiz.why: False. MCSE measures computing error only, not whether the inputs or structure are right.

quiz.q: FiveThirtyEight's 'wins in 71% of simulations' means …
o: the candidate gets 71% of the vote
the candidate won 71% of simulated elections
quiz.why: It is a win probability across simulated outcomes, not a vote share.
